title: the summit sit
hook: the sky going pale over a parking lot, and a Vedic singer who saw the same light and gave it a name

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to jnana, the path of knowing, and a rope that was only ever rope. Did you take one breath and look again before your heart ran off? Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

Early, before the alarm. Out the window, the sky over the parking lot is going from black to gray to something like the inside of a peach. A delivery truck idles. A bird starts, then another. Nobody is going to write a hymn about this particular morning. But on this path, weeks of the year went into hymns that did exactly that, sung to the fire, to the storm, to the dark before creation, and to this light. Today's summit sit climbs back to the Vedas themselves, and to Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `BLACK, GRAY, PEACH.` → `A BIRD, THEN ANOTHER.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, the dawn is a goddess, and the singers talk to her like someone they know. In one hymn, in paraphrase, she wakes every living thing and sends each one off to its own work: one to look for food, one to its task, one to its prayer. She travels the same path every morning, and she never wears out. And then the singer turns a corner. The people who watched the dawns before us are gone, the hymn says. We are the ones seeing her now. And others will come after us who will see her too. That's a hymn about light, and it's also a hymn about being alive for a while. From up here, look at how much of the Vedas stretch was like that. The very first hymn of the Rig Veda calls on Agni, the fire. A singer named Vasishtha asks Varuna why their friendship went cold. A hymn quotes the people who doubt Indra exists, out loud. The hymn of creation ends with or perhaps not. The Sama Veda takes verses and sets them to song. The Atharva Veda sits at a sickbed with a glass of water. And the verse known as the Gayatri turns out to be a verse to Savitr, the sun as the one who sets things moving. The year found that the Vedas aren't only ancient rules. They are people talking to the world as if it could hear: the fire, the water, the dark and the morning. Ushas is one door into all of it. She arrives every day. Nobody has to believe anything to see her come.
screen: `THE DAWN WAKES EVERY LIVING THING.` · `THOSE BEFORE US, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `FIRE, VARUNA, DOUBT, A SICKBED.` · `TALKING TO THE WORLD AS IF IT HEARS.` · then, large: `SHE ARRIVES EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the dawn, wherever you are. Sit, and let the breath come and go. If you can see a window, look at the light in it, whatever time it is. If not, close your eyes and remember the last sunrise you saw. Then bring to mind the people who watched dawns before you: a grandparent, someone gone. Then the people who will see dawns after you. Sit in the middle of that line, here, seeing the light now. If you pray, you can greet the dawn the way the singers did. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the Vedas themselves, and Ushas, the dawn who wakes every living thing. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Tomorrow morning, or the next time you're up early, look at the dawn for one full minute before you look at a screen. Day one thousand four hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Vedic hymns are recited from memory in traditional schools of chanting, and Hindus who keep a morning practice may greet the day with prayers such as the Gayatri, often facing the rising sun.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: uṣas, the dawn, a goddess in the Rig Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Vedas are a list of old rituals.
what it means: they're hymns, people talking to fire, water, dark and dawn as if the world could hear.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 1.113, the hymn to Ushas that sets the singer between the mortals who saw earlier dawns and those who will see later ones.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.1 (to Agni); 7.86 (Vasishtha to Varuna); 2.12 (Indra and the doubters); 10.129 (creation); 3.62.10 (the Gayatri, to Savitr)

notes: Summit sit, day 9: revisits 'The Vedas themselves' (1244–1285), centered on Ushas (1248, 1270).

Rig Veda 1.113 paraphrased: Ushas wakes living things to their various works (seeking food, tasks, worship), goes the same path, does not age; mortals who saw earlier dawns are gone, we see her now, others will see her later. Confirm the verses (approx. 1.113.5–6, 1.113.11).
